fixes.explanation: That's it. Jesus says it's to His Father's glory "…that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples." The fruit shows who they belong to. So the same fruit that proves they're His disciples is to His Father's glory.

Promises are a good thing, but Jesus uses a different word. He says, "If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love…" The word He picks is commandments, and what comes with keeping them is remaining in His love.

Jesus says it Himself: "…just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and remain in His love." He is not asking them to do something He hasn't done. He says it right in the middle of talking about the disciples remaining in His love.

Praying for each other is a good thing, but Jesus doesn't give that as His commandment here. He says, "…that you love one another as I have loved you." He says it again in verse 17: "This is My command to you: Love one another."

Forgiving one another is a good thing, but Jesus doesn't give it as His commandment here. He says, "…that you love one another as I have loved you." He says it again in verse 17: "This is My command to you: Love one another."

Jesus isn't talking about a neighbor here. He's talking about a servant and his master: "…a servant does not understand what his master is doing." Then He tells the disciples, "No longer do I call you servants…"
Jesus isn't comparing a servant to a brother. He's talking about a servant and his master: "…a servant does not understand what his master is doing." Then He says, "But I have called you friends…"

Building a great house is a big project, but Jesus doesn't give it to them here. He says, "…I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain…" The job He names is fruit, and He says it's fruit that will remain.

Gate guard sounds like a job with a whistle and a clipboard, and with this mustache in the way I'd be terrible at it. But Jesus doesn't appoint them to that. He says, "…I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain…" That's the assignment.

Jesus says it Himself: "…My Father is the keeper of the vineyard." So the vine is Jesus and the keeper of the whole vineyard is His Father. Then Jesus says what the keeper does: He cuts off every branch that bears no fruit and prunes every branch that does bear fruit.
Isaiah is a big name to reach for, and I see why you did. But Jesus doesn't bring him up here. He says, "…My Father is the keeper of the vineyard." The Father is the one named as keeper.
Yes. Jesus says, "You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you." The cause He names is His word. He says "already," so He's describing where they are right now.
A sacrifice is a serious thing to bring, so I see why that came to mind. But Jesus doesn't point to one here. He says, "You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you."
Same verb, different address. Jesus doesn't send them to a building. He says, "As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love."

This one is true. First Jesus says, "If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love…" Then He adds, "…just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and remain in His love." So He has kept His Father's commandments and remains in His love.
That's the word. Jesus says, "…a servant does not understand what his master is doing." Then He tells the disciples, "No longer do I call you servants…" So He's not treating them as servants.

Jesus says, "…I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you." The reason is that He's told them everything He learned from His Father. That's why He says He no longer calls them servants.
Close, but Jesus turns it the other way. He says, "You did not choose Me, but I chose you." So the text says the disciples did not choose Him. Choosing Him first isn't what Jesus says.
Moses is a big name, so I see why it came to mind. But Jesus doesn't say to ask in his name. He says to ask the Father "…in My name…"
